cards.q: A bank password has 6 digits. Each digit can be any of 0 to 9, and digits may be repeated. How many different passwords are possible?
cards.why: 6 boxes with 10 options each, and repeats are allowed: 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10⁶ = 1 000 000. (10 × 9 × 8 × … is for no repeats.)
cards.hook: Repeats allowed: every box keeps all its options. Multiply them.

cards.q: A password has 6 digits, each 0 to 9, and digits may be repeated. How many different passwords do not contain any zero?
cards.why: No zero leaves 9 options (1 to 9) for every one of the 6 boxes, repeats still allowed: 9⁶ = 531 441. No zero anywhere, not only in the first box.
cards.hook: No zero: take 0 out of every box, then multiply.

cards.q: Of the 1 000 000 possible 6-digit passwords, 531 441 contain no zero. One password is picked at random. What is the probability that it contains at least one zero?
cards.why: All the passwords that are left have at least one zero: 1 000 000 − 531 441 = 468 559, so P = 468 559 ÷ 1 000 000 = 0.468559 (= 1 − 0.531441).
cards.hook: At least one = 1 − none.

cards.q: What is the quickest correct way to find the probability that a random 6-digit password contains at least one zero?
cards.why: "At least one zero" is every password except those with no zero, so take P(no zero) away from 1. 6 × 0.1 counts passwords with two or more zeros more than once.
cards.hook: At least one? Find P(none), then take it from 1.

cards.q: The bank asks John for 3 of the 6 digits of his password, for example the 2nd, 4th and 5th. In how many different ways can the bank select the three boxes?
cards.why: Boxes 2, 4, 5 are the same pick as 5, 2, 4: not an order, a selection. ⁶C₃ = (6 × 5 × 4) ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 20, or list them: 10 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 20.
cards.hook: Order doesn't matter? Count the orders, then divide by 3 × 2 × 1.

cards.q: The bank picks 3 of the 6 boxes of John's password (for example the 2nd, 4th and 5th). Is this an arrangement or a selection, and why?
wrong: Arrangement: each box holds a digit
Selection: the digits may be repeated
cards.why: Asking for boxes 2, 4, 5 or 5, 2, 4 gets the same three digits, so order doesn't matter: a selection, ⁶C₃ = 20, not 6 × 5 × 4 = 120.
cards.hook: Does swapping the order give something new? No: it's a selection (nCr).

cards.q: A restaurant has 4 starters, 6 main courses and 8 desserts. A meal is one starter, one main course and one dessert. How many different three-course meals are available?
cards.why: Every starter goes with every main, and every pair with every dessert, so multiply: 4 × 6 × 8 = 192. 4 + 6 + 8 = 18 counts dishes, not meals.
cards.hook: One from each group: multiply the group sizes.

cards.q: The restaurant still has its 4 starters and 6 main courses, but some of its 8 desserts have sold out. There are now 120 different three-course meals. How many desserts are still available?
cards.why: Starters × mains × desserts = meals: 4 × 6 × d = 120, so 24d = 120 and d = 5. Check: 4 × 6 × 5 = 120. (3 is how many sold out.)
cards.hook: Same counting rule with the unknown in it: then solve for d.

cards.q: 4 starters, 6 main courses and d desserts give 120 different three-course meals. Which equation finds d?
cards.why: The number of meals is starters × mains × desserts, however many desserts there are, so 4 × 6 × d = 120, giving d = 120 ÷ 24 = 5.
cards.hook: Meals = starters × mains × desserts.

cards.q: In a large population, 1 in 8 people play tennis. Four people are chosen at random. What is the probability that the fourth person chosen is the only one to play tennis?
cards.why: Only the 4th plays: no, no, no, yes. People are independent, so 7/8 × 7/8 × 7/8 × 1/8 = 343/4096 ≈ 0.0837. The question names the person, so no × 4.
cards.hook: Named position (the 4th)? One order only: no × 4.

cards.q: 1 in 8 people play tennis. Four people are chosen. Why is P(the fourth is the only one who plays) just 7/8 × 7/8 × 7/8 × 1/8, with no × 4?
cards.right: The question says which person plays
wrong: Only one of the four people plays
Each person has the same 1/8 chance
cards.why: A × 4 would count the 4 places the one player could be in. Here the player must be the 4th, so only the order no, no, no, yes counts.
cards.hook: "Exactly one": × the number of orders. "Only the 4th": one order.
keys: only the order no, no, no, yes counts

cards.q: 1 in 8 people play tennis. Three people are chosen at random. What is the probability that exactly two of them play tennis?
cards.why: Two play, one doesn't: 1/8 × 1/8 × 7/8 = 7/512 for each order. The non-player can be 1st, 2nd or 3rd, so 3 × 7/512 = 21/512 ≈ 0.041.
cards.hook: Exactly two of three: one order's chance × 3.

cards.q: Three people are chosen and exactly two of them play tennis (T = plays, N = doesn't play). In how many different orders can this happen?
cards.why: The one who doesn't play can be 1st, 2nd or 3rd: TTN, TNT, NTT. So there are 3 orders, each with the same probability.
cards.hook: Not sure how many orders? List them: TTN, TNT, NTT.

cards.q: Find the mean of these 7 numbers, correct to 1 decimal place: 17, 8, 9, 8, 14, 11, 28.
cards.why: Add all 7 numbers, both 8s included: 95. Divide by 7: 95 ÷ 7 = 13.571…, and the next digit (7) rounds up: 13.6.
cards.hook: Mean = total ÷ how many. Every value counts, repeats too.

cards.q: Find the median of these 7 numbers: 17, 8, 9, 8, 14, 11, 28.
cards.why: In order: 8, 8, 9, 11, 14, 17, 28. With 7 numbers the median is the (7 + 1) ÷ 2 = 4th one: 11. (13.6 is the mean.)
cards.hook: Median: put them in order first, then take the middle one.

cards.q: To find the median of 17, 8, 9, 8, 14, 11, 28, what must you do first?
cards.why: The median is the middle value of the ordered list, so sort first: 8, 8, 9, 11, 14, 17, 28. Keep both 8s: every value counts.
cards.hook: Median = middle of the sorted list.

cards.q: The list 8, 8, 9, 11, 14, 17, 28 has median 11. One more number is added, and the new median is 10.5. What number was added?
cards.why: 8 numbers: the median is halfway between the 4th and 5th. The new number x sits between 9 and 11, so (x + 11) ÷ 2 = 10.5, x + 11 = 21, x = 10.
cards.hook: Even count: the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

cards.q: A list of numbers in order now has 8 numbers. Where is its median?
cards.why: (8 + 1) ÷ 2 = 4.5, so the median is halfway between the 4th and 5th numbers of the ordered list: add those two and halve.
cards.hook: Odd count: the middle one. Even count: the average of the middle two.

cards.q: Ben must pick one subject from each group: Group A has 3 subjects, Group B has 4 and Group C has 5. How many different choices of three subjects can he make?
cards.why: Each A subject goes with each B subject and each C subject: 3 × 4 × 5 = 60. 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 is the number of subjects, not of choices.
cards.hook: One from each group: multiply.

cards.q: Groups A, B and C have 3, 4 and 5 subjects, and Ben picks one from each. One extra subject is added to one group. Which group should get it, to give Ben the most choices?
cards.why: Try each: extra in A gives 4 × 4 × 5 = 80, in B 3 × 5 × 5 = 75, in C 3 × 4 × 6 = 72. 80 is the biggest, so Group A.
cards.hook: Test every option and compare: show all three products.

cards.q: Groups A, B and C have 3, 4 and 5 subjects: 60 choices of one from each. One extra subject is added to Group A. How many choices are there now?
cards.why: Group A now has 4: 4 × 4 × 5 = 80. The new subject pairs with every one of the 4 × 5 = 20 B-and-C pairs, so 20 more choices, not 1 more.
cards.hook: One new item adds a choice for every pairing of the other groups.

cards.q: In how many ways can the letters of the word CAMOGIE be arranged?
cards.why: 7 different letters: 7 choices for the 1st place, 6 left for the 2nd, and so on: 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 7! = 5040. No letter repeats, so not 7⁷.
cards.hook: n different things in a row: n! ways.

cards.q: How many arrangements of the letters of CAMOGIE start with M and end with a vowel (A, O, I or E)?
cards.why: Restricted places first: the 1st must be M (1 way), the last a vowel (4 ways). 5 letters are left for the 5 middle places: 5! = 120. 1 × 120 × 4 = 480.
cards.hook: Restricted places first (first, last), then fill the rest.

cards.q: You are counting the arrangements of CAMOGIE that start with M and end with a vowel. Which places should you fill first?
wrong: The places in order, left to right
The places with the most options
cards.why: Places with rules come first: the 1st (only M: 1 way) and the last (a vowel: 4 ways). Then the 5 free letters fill the middle: 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
cards.hook: Rules first, free places last.

cards.q: How many arrangements of 3 different letters can be made from the letters of the word CAMOGIE?
cards.why: 3 places, 7 letters, no letter twice: 7 × 6 × 5 = 210. Stop after 3 places (not 7!), and order counts, so not ⁷C₃ = 35.
cards.hook: r places from n things: n × (n − 1) × … with only r numbers.

cards.q: Scatterplot A: points go down, close to a line. B: points go up, close to a line. C: points go up but are spread out. Match them to r = 0.95, 0.6 and −0.95.
cards.why: A goes down, so it is the negative one: −0.95. B and C go up; B's points hug a line, so B is 0.95, and the spread-out C is 0.6.
cards.hook: Sign = direction. Size = how tightly the points hug a line.

cards.q: Three scatterplots have correlation coefficients 0.95, 0.6 and −0.95. How do you spot the one with r = −0.95?
cards.right: Its points go down from left to right
wrong: Its points are the most spread out
Its points are closest to the x-axis
Its points go up most steeply
cards.why: A negative r means y goes down as x goes up. −0.95 is also close to −1, so its points go downhill and sit close to a straight line.
cards.hook: Minus sign = downhill.
keys: A negative r means y goes down as x goes up

cards.q: Scatterplot B: the points go up and lie close to a straight line, and r = 0.95. What must a full explanation of why 0.95 is right say?
cards.right: Positive, and the points are close to a line
wrong: Positive: as x goes up, y goes up
The points rise along a steep line
There are lots of points in the plot
cards.why: Say both: the direction (as x goes up, y goes up: positive) and the strength (the points lie close to a straight line: strong). So r is close to +1.
cards.hook: Explain r with two things: direction and strength.
